questions.question: In the metric-space definition, what must be true for $\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}$ to be uniformly continuous on $\boldsymbol{X}$?
options: For every point $\boldsymbol{x}\in\boldsymbol{X}$, a different $\delta$ must be chosen after fixing $\boldsymbol{x}$.
The two metric spaces must use the same metric function.
For every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, one $\delta \gt 0$ works for all pairs $\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2\in\boldsymbol{X}$.
The function must be bounded on $\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: Which extra domain condition turns continuity into uniform continuity?
options: Every continuous function between any two metric spaces is uniformly continuous.
Every bounded function between metric spaces is uniformly continuous.
Every continuous function defined on a compact set is uniformly continuous.
Every function into a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.

questions.question: Why is every constant function uniformly continuous between metric spaces?
options: Its input distance is always $0$.
Its output distance is always $0$.
It changes every distance by a factor of $2$.
It is defined only on compact spaces.

questions.question: If $d_X(x_1,x_2) \lt \delta$, what inequality must uniform continuity provide for outputs?
options: $d_X(f(x_1),f(x_2)) \lt \varepsilon$
$d_Y(f(x_1),f(x_2)) \lt \varepsilon$
$d_Y(x_1,x_2) \lt \delta$
$f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ always

questions.question: Let $(X,d_X)$ carry the discrete metric and let $(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space. Which statement about functions $f\colon X\to Y$ is correct?
options: Every function $f\colon X\to Y$ is uniformly continuous.
Only the bounded functions $f\colon X\to Y$ are uniformly continuous.
Every function $f\colon X\to Y$ is continuous, but only the constant ones are uniformly continuous.
Only the functions $f\colon X\to Y$ with finitely many values are uniformly continuous.

questions.question: Let $X$ carry the discrete metric. Why does choosing $\delta=\tfrac12$ show that every function $f\colon X\to Y$ is uniformly continuous, whatever the metric space $Y$?
options: Because every output distance, even between images of distinct input points, is automatically less than $\tfrac12$.
Because $d_X(x_1,x_2)<\tfrac12$ forces $x_1=x_2$, so the output distance is $0$.
Because the codomain $Y$ must then also carry the discrete metric.
Because every function from a discrete space is constant.

questions.question: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be continuous between metric spaces. Which hypothesis on the domain $X$ guarantees that $f$ is uniformly continuous on $X$?
options: $X$ is compact.
$X$ is a bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
$X$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
$X$ is an interval in $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Let $f\colon X\to Y$ be a function between metric spaces and let $A,B\subseteq X$, where uniform continuity of $f$ on a subset uses the metric $d_X$ between points of that subset. Which statement is true for all such $f$, $A$ and $B$?
options: If $f$ is uniformly continuous on $X$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A$.
If $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A$ and on $B$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A\cup B$.
If $f$ is continuous at every point of $A$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A$.
If $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $X$.

questions.question: On $X=(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2})$ let $d(x,y)=|x-y|$ and $d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|$, two metrics with the same open sets. Which statement about the identity map $\operatorname{id}(x)=x$ is correct?
options: Both $\operatorname{id}\colon(X,d)\to(X,d_{\tan})$ and $\operatorname{id}\colon(X,d_{\tan})\to(X,d)$ are uniformly continuous.
Only $\operatorname{id}\colon(X,d)\to(X,d_{\tan})$ is uniformly continuous.
Neither $\operatorname{id}\colon(X,d)\to(X,d_{\tan})$ nor $\operatorname{id}\colon(X,d_{\tan})\to(X,d)$ is uniformly continuous.
Only $\operatorname{id}\colon(X,d_{\tan})\to(X,d)$ is uniformly continuous.

questions.question: Let $f\colon(\mathbb{R}^2,d_\infty)\to(\mathbb{R},|\cdot|)$, $f(x,y)=x+y$, where $d_\infty((x_1,y_1),(x_2,y_2))=\max\{|x_1-x_2|,|y_1-y_2|\}$. Which choice of $\delta$, for every $\varepsilon>0$, guarantees $|f(p)-f(q)|<\varepsilon$ for all $p,q\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $d_\infty(p,q)<\delta$?
options: $\delta=\varepsilon$
$\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2}}$
$\delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$
$\delta=2\varepsilon$
